# Conclusion

Under the increasing threat of urban heat, rising temperatures present a pressing challenge for many regions, calling for urgent and broad-based sustainable cooling solutions (UNEP, 2021). In this context, the role of urban green spaces (UGS) is beyond doubt critical in addressing urban heat and strengthening climate resilience, thereby ensuring fair access to cooling-effective UGS is essential. Otherwise, vulnerable populations may face greater impact, further exacerbating environmental justice (EJ). This study therefore examined how potential accessibility to cooling-effective UGS patterns was related to heat exposure and socioeconomic context in London. By integrating remote sensing (RS), network-based multimodal accessibility and spatial equity analysis, this offered a more comprehensive understanding of whether green spaces capable of providing measurable cooling benefits are also accessible to neighbourhoods with greater heat exposure and relative deprivation. The findings demonstrated substantial variation in both cooling performance and accessibility of UGS across London. Returning to our research question, the answer appears to be that multimodal accessibility to cooling-effective UGS is unevenly distributed across the city, with local inequities varying across heat exposed and socioeconomically deprived areas.  

Overall, these findings contribute to conventional green spaces accessibility and EJ research, demonstrating the importance of considering cooling performance, multi-mode accessibility and spatial patterns of areas of deficiency. Looking forward, addressing these spatial mismatches should involve more considerations towards equalising the benefits of cooling infrastructure and intervention strategies towards areas and communities most needed. Based on London’s evidence, we thus recommend to explicitly considering local cooling access within green infrastructure and heat resilience planning frameworks. With regard to future research, this approach provides a transferable and policy relevant starting point for further analyses. 

All in all, the implications contribute not only towards London’s long-term heat resilience but also supporting wider global initiatives for safe and accessible green spaces and climate adaptation, namely the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 11, 13 and the New Urban Agenda’s commitment for “well-connected and well-distributed networks of open, multipurpose, safe, inclusive, accessible and quality public spaces to improving the resilience of cities to disasters and climate change” (United Nations, 2015; UN Habitat, 2020, p. 19). Ultimately, the success of such policy ambitions in practice also requires collaboration between boroughs and stakeholders to turn spatial evidence into targeted and actionable solutions.
